A casualty is a person who has been killed, injured, or otherwise harmed as a result of an accident, a disaster, a war, or any other violent or dangerous event. The defining idea is this: the harm came from something that happened to them — something outside their control.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

Many learners think "casualty" means "a dead person." That is incomplete. A casualty is anyone who has been killed or injured — both. This is crucial.

Imagine a bomb explodes in a crowded market. 15 people die and 60 people are badly injured. The total number of casualties is 75 — not just 15. All of them — the dead and the injured together — count as casualties.

So whenever you see the word "casualty," remember: it is an umbrella word that covers death and injury together.
The Two Main Senses

1. In war and conflict

This is the most common and most serious use. When soldiers fight, some are killed, some are wounded, some are captured, and some go missing — all of these are counted as "casualties" in military language, because all of them represent people who can no longer fight.

"The battle resulted in heavy casualties on both sides."
"Thousands of civilian casualties were reported during the conflict."

Notice "civilian casualties" — this refers to ordinary people (not soldiers) who are killed or hurt during a war or attack. This phrase comes up very often in news and history.

2. In accidents and disasters

Outside of war, "casualty" is used for people harmed in accidents, natural disasters, fires, explosions, plane crashes, and similar events.

"Fortunately, there were no casualties in the building fire — everyone escaped in time."
"The earthquake caused hundreds of casualties."
The Figurative (Non-Literal) Sense

"Casualty" is also used figuratively — meaning you can apply it to things (not just people) that are destroyed, ruined, or lost as a result of some event or decision.

"The small bookshop was a casualty of the rise of online shopping."
"His friendship with her became a casualty of the bitter argument."
"Truth is often the first casualty of war." (a very famous saying)

In all these cases, something did not literally bleed or die — but it was destroyed, ended, or severely damaged because of some larger force or event. This is a powerful and very common use of the word in writing and speech.
"A Casualty" vs. "Casualties"

• A casualty (singular): one individual person who was killed or injured.

"He was a casualty of the explosion."

  • Casualties (plural): a number of such people, often used when counting or estimating harm.

"The rescue teams worked through the night to reach the casualties."
"Officials reported 200 casualties."

The word is countable, so you can say one casualty, two casualties, heavy casualties, few casualties, mass casualties.
"Heavy Casualties" vs. "Light Casualties"

You will often hear these paired phrases:

  • Heavy casualties = a large number of people killed or injured; severe loss of life.
  • Light casualties = relatively few people killed or injured; the damage was less severe than expected.
A Special British English Use

In British English, "Casualty" (often capitalized) also refers to the emergency department of a hospital — the section where people are taken immediately after accidents or sudden severe illness. Americans call this the "Emergency Room" or "ER." British people say:

"She was rushed to Casualty after the car crash."
"The hospital's Casualty ward was overwhelmed."

This use makes logical sense: a casualty (an injured person) is taken to the Casualty department.
The Tone of the Word

"Casualty" always carries a serious, grave tone. It is not a casual or light word. It appears most frequently in news reports, history books, military briefings, and formal writing. When you encounter it, you are almost always reading or hearing about something tragic — a war, a disaster, a serious accident, or a damaging loss.
Quick Summary

SituationWhat "casualty" means
In a warA soldier or civilian killed, wounded, captured, or missing
In a disaster or accidentA person killed or injured
FigurativelySomething destroyed or ended as a result of a larger event
In British hospitalsThe emergency department
One Final Note

The key insight that separates good understanding of this word from a shallow one: casualty is broader than death. It is a word about loss caused by an external harmful event — whether that loss is a life, a limb, a relationship, a project, or the truth itself.
